title: Is Legal Tech in a Bubble? — Nikki Shaver
pub: AAA — AI and the Future of Law (YouTube)
author: Nikki Shaver

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Shaver accepts the cluster’s core account that AI will reshape delivery economics through outcome-oriented service redesign, in-house adoption, verification costs and AI-native competition. She materially develops it by proposing a focused incumbent strategy: invest deeply in selected expertise and client relationships to provide embedded, continuous AI-enabled services, while treating clients’ insourcing as both a spending threat and an opportunity for new work. She does not address the apprenticeship problem directly, and her disruption and adoption claims remain qualified or anecdotal.
qs: They will be the firms that take very considered, deep, probably expensive bets in key areas of expertise, or areas where they have particularly important clients, and that deliver embedded, continuous services combined with AI in those areas of expertise—and charge for that in a way that enables them to actually increase margins.
Certainly, clients are focused on using AI as a way to decrease outside counsel spend and keep more work in-house.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s business-model framing and materially develops its account of provider convergence: AI-native businesses may scale more readily, product vendors may become legal-service providers, and profitable incumbents may delay adaptation. Its disruption case is illustrative and prospective rather than supported by comparative performance data.
qs: They’ve just launched with a business model that puts AI and tech at the center of it, which is different from incumbent firms that are trying to move toward that but haven’t had it from inception.
That is such a shift in the way legal services are delivered and the players in that market that you could see it as being really quite disruptive.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Shaver accepts the cluster’s operating-model and bargaining-shift thesis, while materially extending it with a selective strategy for differentiated, continuous AI-enabled services and concrete governance requirements for agentic systems. She also reinforces the prospect of greater in-house retention and competition from AI-native service providers, while preserving a role for firms’ distinctive expertise.
qs: They will be the firms that take very considered, deep, probably expensive bets in key areas of expertise, or areas where they have particularly important clients, and that deliver embedded, continuous services combined with AI in those areas of expertise—and charge for that in a way that enables them to actually increase margins.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Shaver accepts that AI value depends on organisational strategy rather than access to common tools, and materially develops the proposition by prescribing selective, expertise-led investment in embedded services alongside careful rollout and governance. Her claims are strategic recommendations and qualified forecasts, not measured evidence of realised transformation.
qs: They will be the firms that take very considered, deep, probably expensive bets in key areas of expertise, or areas where they have particularly important clients, and that deliver embedded, continuous services combined with AI in those areas of expertise—and charge for that in a way that enables them to actually increase margins.
So it’s about having the right controls in place, rolling out carefully, and understanding the risks involved.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Shaver accepts the cluster’s framing of AI adoption as strategic service redesign rather than tool acquisition. She materially develops it by prescribing concentrated investment in expertise-led, embedded AI services, while linking incumbent resistance to profitability and emphasizing governance, security and people costs.
qs: They will be the firms that take very considered, deep, probably expensive bets in key areas of expertise, or areas where they have particularly important clients, and that deliver embedded, continuous services combined with AI in those areas of expertise—and charge for that in a way that enables them to actually increase margins.
And from my perspective, firms are already behind on the governance side.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts that AI-integrated delivery can redraw boundaries between software vendors, legal-service providers and incumbent firms. It materially extends the cluster by identifying AI-native scaling advantages and an innovator’s-dilemma mechanism through which entrants can use established firms as suppliers while competing with them. Its examples remain illustrative rather than comparative performance evidence.
qs: This is a company, for example, that starts out as a product company and then launches a law firm that is services-based, but runs on the underlying AI platform that they initially created.
So they’re a client of those firms, but also leveraging them to disrupt them at the same time.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Shaver accepts the need for selective, workflow-centred deployment and materially extends it with a law-firm strategy: concentrate substantial investment where proprietary expertise, firm and client data, and important relationships can support differentiated continuous services. She also develops the cluster’s risk-based governance proposition by calling for careful agentic rollouts and enforceable controls.
qs: They will be the firms that take very considered, deep, probably expensive bets in key areas of expertise, or areas where they have particularly important clients, and that deliver embedded, continuous services combined with AI in those areas of expertise—and charge for that in a way that enables them to actually increase margins.
So it’s about having the right controls in place, rolling out carefully, and understanding the risks involved.

st.t: AI costs: Time savings obscure delivery economics
st.an: Shaver directly supports the cluster’s central shift from gross time savings or token prices to total delivery economics. She identifies substantial usage costs hidden by bundled legal-AI licences and stresses that sustainable ROI must include continuing expenditure on technology, people and supporting resources. She does not resolve pricing, margin or valuation questions.
qs: So I think the key question is more: how will the investment over time make sense within the firm’s business model, and how will firms be able to accommodate the ongoing investment?
It’s also in the resources and the people you need around it, which are very, very significant.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Shaver strongly aligns with the synthesis: AI reshapes legal-service delivery and economics rather than eliminating lawyers, with selective automation, proprietary expertise, client trust and in-house adoption driving reallocation. She also supports repricing and AI-native competition while retaining uncertainty about which challengers will prevail and emphasising review, security and implementation costs.
qs: They will be the firms that take very considered, deep, probably expensive bets in key areas of expertise, or areas where they have particularly important clients, and that deliver embedded, continuous services combined with AI in those areas of expertise—and charge for that in a way that enables them to actually increase margins.
Certainly, clients are focused on using AI as a way to decrease outside counsel spend and keep more work in-house.

kp.k: AI investment shifts toward quality and repricing
kp.d: Speaking in May 2026, Shaver describes firms moving from experimentation in 2023 through extensive piloting and short-term licensing toward a different ROI debate. Whereas efficiency dominated in 2024 and 2025, she now sees greater attention to advice quality and client outcomes, with measurement still an open question. She reports managing partners taking repricing seriously from around March 2025, after initially avoiding it despite anticipated time savings.
qs: In 2024 and 2025, the focus around ROI was really on efficiency gains.

there is more value in quality: the quality of output, how you can increase the outcome for your clients, how you can increase the effectiveness of the advice for your clients, and how you can give them more.
But in 2025, around March, we started noticing that managing partners were really focused on having those challenging conversations: thinking about pricing, thinking about revaluing legal work.

kp.k: Legal platforms can economize on intensive model usage
kp.d: Shaver rejects a reported Harvey seat price of $1,200 monthly and puts negotiated general-purpose legal platform pricing at approximately $200 to $300 per user per month. She argues that document-heavy legal workflows incur substantial direct token costs, while legal platforms negotiate with frontier labs and currently offer effectively unrestricted usage within licenses. As anecdotal support, she reports firms routing some Claude-related build work through Harvey to save money.
qs: A couple of years ago, someone said the cost of Harvey was something like $1,200 a month. That was never the cost of a seat.
Generally speaking, for these platforms, it’s more like $200 to $300 per month, per user. And that’s obviously negotiated.
Your token use, therefore, is kind of unlimited within those platforms, within your license.
But in order to save money, they’re taking some of that and running it through Harvey, because it’s cheaper to do that than to use Claude.

kp.k: Strategic technology spending includes people, security, and review
kp.d: Shaver contrasts technology's former support status with its current strategic role in client delivery. She emphasizes investment in supporting personnel and managing risks from both internally deployed AI and material received from others. She predicts lower token costs but remains uncertain whether overall platform investment will fall, expecting firms to adapt pricing to accommodate technology and staffing costs.
qs: IT was typically seen as foundational support. Now it’s seen as hugely strategic, which means managing partners are willing and eager to invest because they see it as part of their delivery model for clients.
Especially because the investment is not just in the technology. It’s also in the resources and the people you need around it, which are very, very significant.
So will token costs come down over time? I’m sure they will. Will the investment in those platforms overall come down? I’m not sure.

kp.d: Using the innovator's dilemma framework, Shaver argues that incumbent profitability can suppress urgency precisely when new providers gain ground. She distinguishes firms designed around AI from technology companies launching service-delivering law firms on their own platforms, citing Eudia Law or Eudia Counsel. She describes General Legal as automating about 80% of the law while outsourcing the highest-end work to top-tier firms, making those firms suppliers to a potential disruptor. She explicitly leaves uncertain which entrants will ultimately disrupt the market.
qs: It’s really hard at the moment to tell who the disruptors are going to be, and whether they are, in fact, going to be the AI-native firms.
The key, of course, for the innovator’s dilemma is that as law firms see their bottom line continue to grow, there’s no urgency for them to shift the way they’re doing things.

I think the model of General Legal—which was founded by some very experienced founders from legal tech—is quite interesting, where they’re automating about 80% of the law and then sending the top-cream legal work out to top-tier law firms.
So they’re a client of those firms, but also leveraging them to disrupt them at the same time.

kp.k: Procurement should follow use cases and continuous experimentation
kp.d: Shaver recommends selecting tools against concrete problems, whether contract-data extraction or broad lawyer AI fluency, rather than novelty or competitor choices. Integration requirements, user preferences, jurisdictions, and languages narrow the field. Drawing an analogy with R&D departments outside law firms, she recommends a dedicated experimentation budget alongside deployment of existing tools to validate usefulness and maintain internal literacy.
qs: For me, the advice I always have is that it still comes back to the problem you’re trying to solve or the use case you’re trying to address.

Once you’ve looked at that and your own systems environment—the integrations you would need, the preferences your people have, the jurisdictions in which you operate, the languages in which you need this to operate—it reduces significantly the number of products you’re looking at.
You need to actually be experimenting on an ongoing basis at the same time as you’re deploying and getting value out of the tools already in your tech stack.

kp.k: Tracked market growth shows no bubble bursting
kp.d: Shaver reports that Legaltech Hub's legal AI and generative AI maps show about 100 net new companies every quarter, after removing acquisitions and business closures, with the forthcoming June 2026 map on a similar trajectory. She interprets this steady growth into generative AI's third or fourth year as inconsistent with a conventional rapid-expansion-and-collapse bubble, while stopping short of ruling out a bubble. This is her interpretation of directory tracking, not a valuation study.
qs: First of all, if it is a bubble currently, it shows no sign of bursting.
It’s about 100 new companies every quarter. That has been very steady.
And when I say 100 new, I mean having already controlled for M&A in the market and companies that have gone out of business, which we remove from the map and from our active directory.
So to me, that indicates that if it’s a bubble, it’s a very sustained one, which is unusual.

kp.k: Technology becomes inseparable from legal practice and training
kp.d: Shaver uses e-discovery as an analogy for technology becoming integral to both legal work and learning to perform it. She predicts similar integration in due diligence and across practice areas. Her expectation that around 80% of legal work will be automated supports her argument for structurally higher technology spending; the transcript supplies no study or methodology for that estimate.
qs: In order to learn how to do discovery in a law firm now, you also have to learn how to use the tools that allow you to do that work.
If you’re an M&A lawyer, when you learn about due diligence, you won’t just learn about the actual legal requirements around due diligence. You will also learn about the technology that powers it.

If you look at what’s likely in terms of how much legal work will be automated, it’s a very significant percentage. It’s up around 80%, which means there just has to be fundamentally a bigger spend and a bigger investment in technology to support it.

kp.k: Growing demand can coexist with consolidation and failures
kp.d: Shaver expects substantially more M&A and eventual startup failures even as aggregate demand for legal technology grows. She reports already seeing competitive pressure prompt some startups to seek early exits. Her position is therefore not that continued net growth guarantees individual provider survival.
qs: On the other hand, I also believe that M&A will increase considerably. We’ll see more consolidation.
We’re already seeing pressure on some startups in the market where they’re seeking early exits because it’s just been such a difficult competitive space to be in.
But I do think overall, we’ll continue to need more.

kp.d: Shaver argues that deploying the same platforms as competitors does not differentiate firms. She predicts stronger results from selective, deep investment in distinctive expertise or important client relationships than from spreading workflow-building resources across every practice. Her proposed model combines proprietary expertise and data with AI-enabled, continuous services priced for higher margins rather than competing solely on cheaper automated work.
qs: The firms that are going to win this are not going to be the ones that broadly try to deploy and create internal workflows across every single practice of their firm and spend all their resources doing that.

They will be the firms that take very considered, deep, probably expensive bets in key areas of expertise, or areas where they have particularly important clients, and that deliver embedded, continuous services combined with AI in those areas of expertise—and charge for that in a way that enables them to actually increase margins.
It is about delivering something highly differentiated because of your firm’s expertise and data for key clients at top-rate margins.

kp.k: In-house adoption threatens spend but creates firm opportunities
kp.d: Responding to McCormack's suggestion that clients can build equally easily, Shaver argues that firms possess expertise and data unavailable to clients except through partner advice. She reports a doubling over the preceding year, ambiguously referring either to AI-enabled client work or departments using AI, without specifying a dataset. She acknowledges pressure to retain work in-house but reports firm clients taking previously declined high-volume work through AI. She also recommends trusted-adviser and workflow co-building services to strengthen client relationships.
qs: I’m talking about baking in your expertise to a delivery system that combines your law firm’s data and expertise with key client data and delivers targeted, ongoing advice to them, that is super high value on a continuous basis.

The amount of work that clients are now doing with AI—or the amount of in-house departments that are leveraging AI—has doubled in the past year, which is a very significant trend, although they were behind initially.
In fact, I’ve had a number of clients say, “We are now taking on work that previously we didn’t, because we can without it taking time away from the high-value work that we want our partners to do.”
The other way is by working with your clients to be their trusted advisors around automation and AI.

kp.k: Agent adoption remains early despite market rhetoric
kp.d: Shaver initially rejects the picture of lawyers orchestrating agents, while acknowledging cautious deployment of agentic tools. She subsequently clarifies that she means orchestration as a platform layer coordinating models, not merely lawyers using agentic products, which she agrees is occurring. She distinguishes autonomous agents with tools and end-to-end task execution from hard-coded workflows lacking autonomy; this distinction matters for security risk.
qs: There’s a big disconnect between what we hear in the market around agentic AI and actual agents being deployed.

When I think of orchestration in the context of AI, I think of an orchestration layer within a platform where it is pulling together outputs from many models into what actually goes to the lawyer or end user.
Whether lawyers are actually using agentic AI—yes, I’m sure they are.

An AI agent has autonomy and access to tools. It is able to undertake a full end-to-end workflow using those tools, deciding which tools make the most sense within that workflow, and understanding when it has come to an end.

kp.k: Agent autonomy requires enforceable governance and renewed security review
kp.d: Shaver says firms are already behind on governance amid fragmented, changing regulation, professional requirements, and client restrictions. She regards manual checks of client AI prohibitions as unsustainable. Reported firm conversations illustrate the need for unique agent identifiers; connected agents also raise questions about downstream data access and models. She recommends careful rollout, technical policy enforcement, and revisiting provider security reviews when platforms add agentic capabilities rather than relying on pre-agent approval.
qs: And from my perspective, firms are already behind on the governance side.
Then they realized, “We’re in a place now where we need unique identifiers for agents in our systems.”
What is the data that a downstream agent has access to, and how is that maintained? What models are being used in the back end? Is that compliant with all of your guidelines and security policies?

Really, law firms should be going back and revisiting security with the provider to ensure that additional questions are asked about how autonomy is handled within the system, what access the agents have to other systems, and so on.
The thing that is really important for firms to know, too, is that there are now AI governance technologies you can deploy to enforce your policies and other rules internally.

kp.k: Next-year forecasts emphasize agents and interconnected platforms
kp.d: Looking one year ahead from May 2026, Shaver forecasts consolidation and more commonplace agentic AI, while presenting an unexpected major-provider failure and a legal-tech IPO as possibilities. She expects Model Context Protocol or similar standards to simplify connections between frontier models and legal providers, with Harvey or Anthropic Claude potentially acting as front interfaces through which users access other providers' capabilities.
qs: We may see at least one major provider fail in a way that we didn’t expect.
We might see an IPO in the legal tech market.
We’ll see far more agentic AI, and we’ll see that become far more common.
MCP is Model Context Protocol.
So I think we’ll see Harvey as the front layer, with the ability to pull capabilities from a lot of legal tech startups. I think we’ll see Anthropic Claude as a front layer.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nikki Shaver says firms are shifting AI investment discussions from efficiency toward quality, client outcomes and repricing legal work.
pts.d: Shaver describes a progression from experimentation in 2023 to simultaneous platform pilots and short-term licensing, with piloting and short-term commitments continuing because technology changes quickly. By May 2026, she observes greater attention to measuring better advice and outcomes rather than simply time saved. She dates more serious managing-partner discussions about pricing and revaluing work to approximately March 2025. These are observations from her market-facing work, not findings from a specified survey.

pts.k: Shaver expects token costs to fall but does not expect that necessarily to reduce firms’ overall AI investment; she predicts pricing will adapt to technology and people costs.
pts.d: Shaver puts negotiated legal-platform prices generally at $200–$300 per user per month and rejects a reported $1,200 Harvey seat price. She says document-heavy legal workflows can make direct frontier-model token usage expensive, while legal applications negotiate with model laboratories and absorb usage within licenses. Her example is unnamed firms routing some Claude-related build work through Harvey to save money. She says technology has become strategically central rather than foundational support, and that investment includes significant staffing, security and human review of AI material received both internally and from other parties. Her cost forecasts have no specific horizon.

pts.k: Shaver identifies AI-native legal-service businesses as potential disruptors, while explicitly withholding certainty about which businesses will disrupt incumbents.
pts.d: She argues that firms designed around AI from inception can scale more easily than incumbents retrofitting their models. Technology companies launching service-delivering law firms represent a potentially disruptive change in market participants, distinct from simply selling legal software. She names Eudia Law/Eudia Counsel and describes General Legal as automating about 80% of legal work while referring the highest-end work to top-tier firms. That percentage is her account of a particular business model, not an independently demonstrated performance result. She invokes the innovator’s dilemma: growing incumbent profits weaken urgency precisely when entrants may establish themselves.

pts.k: Shaver says continuing net growth in legal AI suppliers shows no current sign of a bubble bursting, while expecting consolidation and failures alongside sustained demand.
pts.d: Shaver cites Legaltech Hub’s legal AI and generative AI maps, published since the previous year, as showing approximately 100 net new companies per quarter after removing acquisitions and business closures. In May 2026 she expects the June update to show a similar increase. She interprets that steady trajectory as inconsistent with a conventional boom-and-collapse pattern, but does not definitively rule out a bubble. She also reports early-exit pressure on some startups and forecasts considerably more M&A and gradual failures. Her supplier-count evidence and her interpretation of bubble dynamics are distinct.

pts.k: Shaver predicts that technology will become inseparable from practice-specific legal work and training, with substantial automation requiring structurally greater technology spending.
pts.d: She uses e-discovery as an analogy for the integration she expects across practice areas: learning due diligence, for example, will include learning the technology that powers it. She cites Practical Law’s e-discovery technology units as an existing illustration. Separately from her General Legal example, she forecasts automation of around 80% of legal work overall. No study, calculation, task definition or deadline is supplied for that broader percentage. She connects this forecast to greater technology investment across every practice, rather than making an explicit employment-reduction forecast.

pts.k: Shaver argues that rapid AI development requires continuing experimentation and requirements-led procurement, rather than chasing products or relying on one internal market watcher.
pts.d: Her prescription is to narrow technology selection by the problem being solved, integrations, user preferences, jurisdictions and languages. She argues that a dedicated R&D budget and ongoing experimentation are necessary to maintain AI fluency while obtaining value from existing tools. This is advisory judgment grounded in her technology-selection work; she offers no comparative study of procurement outcomes. Legaltech Hub itself provides the market tracking and selection services she discusses.

pts.k: Shaver predicts competitive advantage will come from focused, proprietary AI-enabled services built around firm expertise and data, not generic platform adoption or indiscriminate internal workflow building.
pts.d: She expects successful firms to make selective, potentially expensive investments in areas of distinctive expertise or important client relationships. These would produce embedded, continuous services priced to increase margins, rather than competing only on cheaper automated work. She says firm knowledge unavailable to clients except through senior partners can be combined with client data to deliver continuing high-value advice. This is a strategic prediction; she reports increased building and some firms understanding the approach but names no tested commercial example or margin result.

pts.k: Shaver says in-house AI use threatens outside-counsel revenue but also allows firms to capture previously unattractive work and offer client automation services.
pts.d: She states that either the amount of client work performed with AI or the number of in-house departments using it has doubled in the preceding year; her wording leaves the precise metric unresolved, and she identifies no dataset. She says corporate clients seek lower external spend and more insourcing. Conversely, AI lets firms accept commoditized, high-volume work without diverting partners from high-value matters. Her support includes accounts from unnamed advisory clients. She also observes firms using operations centers, consulting and co-built workflows to serve clients and retain work.

pts.k: Shaver distinguishes early, cautious agentic deployment from claims of lawyers orchestrating agents, and says autonomy substantially increases governance and security requirements.
pts.d: At the interview date, Shaver sees a disconnect between market rhetoric and deployment. She initially says lawyers are not orchestrating agents, then clarifies that she means orchestration layers coordinating or selecting models, not that lawyers never use agentic tools. She acknowledges agentic functionality within existing providers. She says fragmented regulation, professional rules and client restrictions already strain governance, and agents add issues of identity, downstream access, models and autonomous tool use. Unnamed firm conversations about activity later identified as an agent illustrate her concern. She distinguishes autonomous agents from hard-coded workflows and recommends renewed security review when licensed platforms add agents.

pts.k: Shaver predicts more agentic AI, automated governance and interconnected platform ecosystems over the following year, alongside possible major-provider failure and a legal-tech IPO.
pts.d: In the closing forecast, the horizon is approximately May 2026 to May 2027. Shaver expects consolidation and much more common agentic AI; she presents an unexpected major-provider failure and an IPO as possibilities, not certainties. She expects MCP or similar standards to connect frontier models and legal providers, with Harvey, Legora and Claude acting as interfaces through which users access other providers’ capabilities. She also expects greater adoption of AI governance technology over the next year, noting that only some firms are currently exploring it. These are forward-looking judgments, not demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source chiefly relies on Shaver’s market tracking, advisory experience, named business examples and strategic reasoning, with limited specified quantitative evidence.
pts.d: The clearest quantitative evidence is Legaltech Hub’s reported quarterly net supplier growth, with M&A and closures removed. Pricing estimates, routing work through Harvey, startup exit pressure, changing partner priorities, client service expansion and agent-identification problems are supported by her experience or unnamed firm conversations. Eudia and General Legal illustrate proposed competitive models; e-discovery illustrates technology integration. The broad 80% automation forecast and the ambiguously defined doubling of in-house AI activity have no identified underlying study. No model benchmarks, legal-output quality measurements or quantified margin studies are supplied. Shaver is the co-founder and CEO of the directory and advisory business whose tracking and services she cites.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview is situated in May 2026; it separates retrospective adoption changes, current observations and approximately one-year predictions.
pts.d: The retrospective sequence begins with 2023 experimentation, followed by 2024–2025 efficiency-focused ROI and pricing discussions becoming serious around March 2025. Current claims concern May 2026, with a June market-map update anticipated. The in-house doubling refers to the preceding year, without a precise measurement period. Closing market and integration predictions concern the next year, as does increased governance-tool uptake. Falling token costs, pervasive practice integration and broad automation have no fixed deadline. Conditions include continuing rapid technical change, careful agent controls, suitable security, firm-specific expertise and data, targeted investment, and pricing that supports margins. Shaver explicitly qualifies who will disrupt incumbents, whether total platform spending will fall, whether the market is a bubble, and whether a failure or IPO will occur.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are incumbent firms, AI-native service providers, corporate legal departments, legal-tech vendors, and the lawyers and operational teams implementing AI.
pts.d: Managing partners face investment and pricing choices; incumbent and top-tier firms face both AI-native competition and opportunities for higher-margin continuous services and high-volume work. Corporate legal departments can build internally and reduce outside-counsel spend, while also buying firm expertise and automation assistance. AI-native legal-service businesses may scale through technology-centered delivery; software providers face consolidation, failure and integration into larger interfaces. Lawyers must learn practice-specific technology, while technology, procurement, security and governance teams face ongoing experimentation, vendor review and access-control responsibilities. Shaver discusses supporting people costs but makes no concrete prediction about associate headcount, staffing shape or employment losses. The interview does not advance a specific access-to-justice claim.
